claim: Every animal that bears live young suckles them; every egg-layer gathers food for its young; the exception is the bat, which lays eggs and yet suckles.
lewysohn: §§ 16 and 136 (pp. 9, 104): calls the egg-laying claim false and "striking"; says the Talmud followed Scripture, which lists the bat among birds. He also limits the first half: some insects and the viper bear live young but do not suckle.
modern: All bats (order Chiroptera, about 1,400 species) are placental mammals. They are viviparous and suckle with mammary glands. No bat lays eggs. The only egg-laying mammals are the monotremes (platypus, echidnas), which also produce milk. The rule "live-bearer suckles" is also false outside mammals: many sharks, snakes (vipers) and some insects bear live young without milk.
verdict_note: Suckling: true. Egg-laying: false. Lewysohn's correction is right.
lewysohn_short: Right: bats do not lay eggs

claim: A cat gives birth after 52 days (in the same list: a dog after 50 days).
lewysohn: §§ 17, 118 (pp. 10, 75–76): "inexact", because the cat carries 55 days (Voigt); at § 118 he calls 52 days "fairly accurate".
modern: Domestic cat gestation averages about 65 days (studies: 65.1 d in 1,056 UK pedigree litters; 65.3 d, range 57–72; 66.9 d in a research colony). 52 days is at the extreme low edge of reported ranges and is about 13 days short of the mean. The dog figure (50 days) is also short: dogs average about 63 days from ovulation (roughly 57–72 days from mating).
verdict_note: Off by about 20%. Lewysohn's 55 days (from Voigt, 1835–40) is also too short.
lewysohn_short: Calls it inexact; his own 55 d is also too short

claim: A pig gives birth after 60 days.
lewysohn: §§ 17, 170 (pp. 10, 147): repeats the figure; no correction.
modern: Domestic pig (Sus scrofa domesticus) gestation is about 114 days (the farmers' rule "3 months, 3 weeks, 3 days"); large commercial herds now average up to about 117 days.
verdict_note: Almost half the real length. Lewysohn missed the error.

claim: The wolf, lion, bear, leopard, bardelas (hyena?), elephant, monkey and kipof (long-tailed ape) give birth after three years.
lewysohn: § 17 (pp. 10–11) and at each animal: "erroneous"; traces the figure to Aristotle (elephant 18 months to 3 years) and to popular belief, because these animals' mating is rarely seen.
modern: Wolf about 63 days; lion about 108–110 days; leopard about 90–105 days; brown bear about 7 months from mating, because the embryo rests for 4–5 months before implantation (active gestation about 56 days); spotted hyena about 110 days, striped hyena about 90 days; African elephant about 22 months (the longest of any living mammal); macaques about 5.5 months. None reaches three years.
verdict_note: Wrong by a factor of 5–17 for every animal except the elephant (wrong by about 40%). Lewysohn is right, and his source (Aristotle) is the likely origin.

claim: Small kosher livestock (sheep, goats) give birth after 5 months; large kosher livestock (cattle) after 9 months; large non-kosher livestock (donkey, camel, horse) after 12 months.
lewysohn: § 17 (p. 11): correct for domestic animals whose mating is watched; agrees with Aristotle (sheep and goat 5 months, mare 11–12 months). But he says the 12-month rule "cannot apply to the camel", which Aristotle says carries five months.
modern: Sheep about 147 days and goat about 150 days (= 5 months). Cattle about 283 days (= 9.3 months). Horse about 340 days (11 months), donkey about 365–375 days (12 months), dromedary camel about 375–390 days (12–13 months).
verdict_note: Good observational data for herd animals. Here the Talmud is right and Lewysohn's objection is wrong: the camel does carry about 12–13 months; Aristotle's 5 months is the error.
lewysohn_short: Right on livestock; wrong to reject the camel's 12 months

topic: No upper front teeth = ruminant with cloven hooves
claim: Any animal that chews the cud has no upper front teeth; and any animal without upper front teeth chews the cud and has cloven hooves (so Rav Hisda can check a hoof-less carcass by its mouth). The exception is the camel, which has canine-like upper teeth (and the young camel, which does not have them yet).
lewysohn: § 58 (p. 35) and § 163 (p. 135): repeats the rule and the camel exception; explains the camel's "teeth" as dental papillae or gums (Rashi).
modern: Correct for the domain the Talmud means (hoofed livestock). All living true ruminants (suborder Ruminantia: cattle, sheep, goats, deer, antelopes, giraffes) have no upper incisors; a horny dental pad replaces them. Camelids (Tylopoda) chew the cud but are not true ruminants; adults keep one pair of upper incisors (I3), which are cone-shaped and canine-like, plus true upper canines. So the camel exception is anatomically exact. The 'young camel' point is weaker: dental surveys give deciduous upper incisors that erupt within the first weeks or months. Outside livestock the rule fails (sloths, anteaters, pangolins and baleen whales also lack upper incisors), but the Talmud limits it to behema.
verdict_note: A sound diagnostic rule, and the camel exception is a real anatomical observation. The young-camel detail is doubtful.

claim: The hyrax (shafan) and the hare (arnevet) chew the cud, yet have upper front teeth.
lewysohn: §§ 141–142 (pp. 109–111): the hare has upper teeth (true) and "rumination in hares undoubtedly takes place"; rejects Buffon's doubt.
modern: Upper teeth: true. Hares and rabbits have two pairs of upper incisors (the second, small 'peg teeth' behind the first), which is why they are called Lagomorpha, not rodents. Cud-chewing: false in the technical sense. Lagomorphs are hindgut fermenters with one simple stomach. They practise caecotrophy: they eat soft faecal pellets (caecotropes) from the anus, mostly at night. This is sometimes called 'pseudo-rumination', but no food is regurgitated. Hyraxes also do not regurgitate; their jaw movement while resting looks like chewing.
verdict_note: Upper teeth: correct. Rumination: not in the modern sense; caecotrophy is a functional analogue. Lewysohn (and Buffon's critics) were wrong.

topic: Male hyena becomes a bat after 7 years
claim: A male hyena after seven years becomes an atalef (bat); the bat after seven years an arpad; then a thistle, a briar, and finally a demon.
lewysohn: § 119 (pp. 76–77): a "fable" from the ancient belief that the hyena changes its sex (Pliny, Aelian; Aristotle denied it). He reads it as an ethical allegory. He explains the belief by Aristotle's note on a pouch under the tail that looks like a vulva.
modern: False. Hyenas do not change sex or species. All four species (spotted, striped, brown hyena, aardwolf) are gonochoristic: each animal is male or female for life. The sex-change myth has two real sources: the female spotted hyena (Crocuta crocuta) has a pseudo-penis and pseudo-scrotum, so the sexes look alike; and the striped hyena (Hyaena hyaena, the species of the Levant and Mesopotamia) has a large anal (subcaudal) scent pouch that it everts, which is what Aristotle described. Bats, plants and hyenas are of course separate lineages.
verdict_note: Folklore. Lewysohn's explanation, after Aristotle, matches the modern explanation of the striped hyena's anal pouch.
lewysohn_short: Right: a fable; explains it via the hyena's anal pouch

claim: Rav Yehuda: the ishut, a field pest that people may trap on the intermediate festival days, is "a creature that has no eyes" (with Psalm 58:9, "has not seen the sun").
lewysohn: § 135 (pp. 101–102): the Syrian mole, which has no visible eyes; Aristotle found imperfect eyes under the skin. He separates it from the European mole.
modern: True for the animal of the region. The Middle Eastern blind mole-rat (Spalax / Nannospalax ehrenbergi complex, a rodent, not a true mole) has tiny eyes (under 1 mm) completely covered by skin and fur, with no external opening. It is behaviourally blind: no image vision. The buried eye still senses light and sets the circadian and seasonal rhythm. It is exactly the root- and tuber-eating field pest the Mishnah describes. (True moles, Talpidae, do not live in Israel; European moles have small but visible, functional eyes.)
verdict_note: A good field observation. Aristotle's 'eyes under the skin' (followed by Lewysohn) is also correct.
lewysohn_short: Right: Syrian mole, eyes under the skin

claim: Abaye: a deep voice means the dam was a donkey (= hinny); a shrill voice means the dam was a mare (= mule). Rav Pappa: large ears and a small tail mean a donkey dam (hinny); small ears and a large tail mean a mare dam (mule).
lewysohn: § 168 (p. 144): repeats it without comment: the hinny has "a coarser voice, longer ears and a shorter tail".
modern: Mostly the reverse of current descriptions. Breed societies and equine charities say the hinny (horse sire, donkey dam) usually has shorter ears and a more horse-like head, and the mule (donkey sire, mare dam) longer, donkey-like ears; that is, ear length follows the sire more than the dam. Tail descriptions disagree between sources. Voice is not a reliable sign: both usually bray, often with a whinny mixed in. Experts also say appearance alone cannot identify a mule or hinny with confidence; only pedigree or DNA can. The Gemara itself notes cases (a mute animal with docked ears and tail) where the signs fail.
verdict_note: The ear sign is inverted against modern descriptions; the voice and tail signs are unreliable. Evidence is descriptive (breeders, sanctuaries), not controlled study, so rate with care.

claim: The hen (gives birth) at 21 days.
lewysohn: § 17 (pp. 9–10): rejects Rashi (21 days of egg formation inside the hen); the Talmud means the hatching of the chicks on the 20th or 21st day. He says the egg itself is mostly formed within 10 days (Aristotle).
lewysohn_short: Right: means hatching, not egg formation
modern: Chicken eggs hatch after 21 days of incubation (range about 20–22 days, with temperature). Rashi's reading is wrong: the egg passes through the oviduct in about 24–26 hours; before that the yolk grows in the ovary for about 7–10 days, which matches Lewysohn's (Aristotle's) '10 days'.
verdict_note: Exact for incubation. Lewysohn's reading is the right one.

claim: The fox and all kinds of sheratzim (small creatures) give birth after six months.
lewysohn: §§ 17, 120 (pp. 10, 78): repeats it; takes sheratzim here as small predators (weasel, marten).
modern: Red fox gestation is about 52 days (49–58), not 6 months. For Lewysohn's weasel group the answer is mixed: the least weasel carries about 35 days, but the stoat has delayed implantation, so the time from mating to birth is up to about 9–11 months (active fetal growth 3–4 weeks); martens also have delayed implantation. No species fits 6 months as a rule.
verdict_note: Wrong by more than 3 times for the fox. Lewysohn missed it.

claim: The efeh (viper) gives birth after 70 years; the snake after 7 years.
lewysohn: § 17 (p. 10): among "the latter false ones"; traces them to Aristotle's errors and to lack of observation.
modern: Egg-laying snakes incubate their eggs for about 1.5–3 months. Live-bearing vipers such as the adder carry about 4.5 months. In cold climates many female adders breed only every second or third year, but no snake has a gestation of years. Snakes reach maturity in about 2–5 years.
verdict_note: Not close. Lewysohn is right.

topic: Mates by night, births by night (bat); by day (hen)
claim: Any species that mates by day gives birth by day (the hen); any species that mates by night gives birth by night (the bat); a species that mates by day or night (man) gives birth by day or night.
lewysohn: §§ 16, 136 (pp. 9, 103): states it as a rule for nocturnal and diurnal animals; repeats it for the bat.
modern: Hen: true. Hens lay in daylight, mostly in the morning. Bat: probably false. Bats give birth in the roost, where they spend the day; direct records (captive pipistrelles, big brown bats) put births in daytime. Many temperate bats also mate in autumn and winter roosts, partly by day, with sperm storage until spring. As a rule the link is false: the timing of birth does not follow the timing of mating. The mare, a day-active animal, foals at night in about 80% of cases.
verdict_note: Correct for the hen only. The bat example is probably the wrong way round.

claim: Five signs of a mad dog: its mouth is open, its saliva drips, its ears droop, its tail rests on its thighs, it walks at the edges of roads. Some say it also barks with no sound heard.
lewysohn: §§ 38, 122 (pp. 24, 85): repeats all the signs; explains the open mouth by "swelling" of the mouth muscles.
lewysohn_short: Repeats it; wrong cause for the open mouth
modern: Mostly correct for canine rabies. In 'dumb' (paralytic) rabies the jaw muscles are paralysed, so the jaw hangs open; paralysis of the throat stops swallowing, so saliva drips; paralysis of the larynx makes the bark hoarse or silent. Restless wandering is typical. Drooping ears and a tucked tail are general signs of a sick or fearful dog, not specific to rabies. Lewysohn's cause (swelling) is wrong: it is paralysis.
verdict_note: A good clinical description, especially the dropped jaw, drooling and silent bark.

topic: Food stays in a dog's gut 3 days
claim: God knows the dog's food is scarce, so its food stays in its intestines three days (with the Mishnah: food stays undigested in a dog three full days).
lewysohn: § 122 (p. 83): repeats it, but cites "B. batra 8a"; the Sefaria text of Bava Batra 8a does not have it.
lewysohn_short: Repeats it; his citation is wrong
modern: In healthy dogs the stomach empties in about 7–15 hours (capsule studies) and total gut transit is about 1–2.5 days. Undigested bone can stay longer. Three days is at or beyond the upper end, and food is not 'undigested' for that time.
verdict_note: Too long, but the right order of magnitude for the slowest dogs. Dogs do tolerate long gaps between meals, which may be the observation behind it.

claim: We would learn modesty from the cat (which covers its excrement), honesty from the ant, fidelity from the dove, and courtship from the rooster.
lewysohn: §§ 118, 137 (pp. 75, 106): reports it; adds Pliny's reason: the cat hides the smell so that mice are not driven away.
modern: True as behaviour. Domestic cats and their wild ancestor (Felis lybica) usually bury faeces near their home area. Far from home, at territory edges, they often leave them uncovered as scent marks. The reason is scent control, not modesty; Pliny's 'not to scare the mice' is not supported.
verdict_note: The behaviour is correct; the moral is the Talmud's own frame. (The ant, dove and rooster parts are left for the next batch.)

topic: Goats lead; camel's short tail; ox's long tail
claim: Goats walk at the head of the flock and the ewes follow. The camel's tail is short because it eats thorns. The ox's tail is long because it lives in marshes and must drive away gnats.
lewysohn: §§ 52, 155, 160 (pp. 32, 124, 130): repeats all three; gives the goats' lead to their courage.
modern: Goats leading: true. In mixed flocks goats are bolder and more exploratory, and shepherds use them as leaders. Ox tail: true as a function. Cattle use tail switching as their main defence against biting flies. Camel tail: the tail is fairly short (about 50 cm) and the camel does browse on thorny shrubs, but 'so that it does not catch in thorns' is an untested just-so explanation.
verdict_note: Observations correct; the camel reason cannot be tested.

topic: The hen's lower eyelid closes upward
claim: The hen's lower eyelid rises over the upper one, because it lives on rafters and smoke would otherwise blind it.
lewysohn: §§ 46, 79 (pp. 29, 47): repeats it and widens it to "all heavy land birds".
lewysohn_short: Right; widens it to other birds
modern: True. In chickens and most birds the lower eyelid is the larger, more mobile one and closes the eye by moving up (owls are an exception). Birds also have a nictitating membrane that sweeps across the eye. The smoke reason is a just-so explanation; the trait is general to birds.
verdict_note: Anatomy correct. Lewysohn's wider rule is closer to the truth than the Talmud's (it is not limited to heavy birds either).

topic: Fish, snake and pig get stronger with age
claim: Three creatures gain strength as they grow old: the fish, the snake and the pig.
lewysohn: §§ 41, 170 (pp. 26, 147): repeats it; adds (Avodah Zarah 30b) that old snakes have weaker venom.
modern: Fish and snakes: largely true. Both have indeterminate growth: they keep growing after maturity, so old individuals are larger and, in fish, much more fertile (big old females produce far more eggs). Some fish species show almost no ageing. Pig: partly true. Pigs keep gaining weight for several years, and a boar's tusks grow all its life, so an old boar is more dangerous. But pigs do age and decline; they do not have indeterminate growth.
verdict_note: A real biological pattern for fish and snakes; less so for the pig.
